newsitem.title: USA: Americans' health improving, insurer's study finds.
newsitem.headline: Americans' health improving, insurer's study finds.

text.p: Americans' health has improved since 1990 based on measures of access to medical care and mortality but increasing smoking and obesity may bode ill for the nation's well-being, a study said Tuesday.

The overall health score of Americans has climbed 3.6 percent since 1990, according to the detailed study ranking the health of populations in every state by Minnesota insurer ReliaStar Financial Corp.
But this year's "ominous" rise in the U.S. smoking rate to 22.6 percent of the population from 22.2 percent -- an increase of one million smokers -- reversed a declining trend.

"The personal decisions everyone makes about behaviour and nutrition make a difference. And nothing reflects the importance of healthy choices more than the decision about whether to use tobacco," ReliaStar vice president Dan McCormick said.
"Americans are spending more money than ever before on health care, but the simple truth is that we can't buy our way out of taking personal responsibility for health," he said.

In a warning of health problems to come, the study cited a recent University of Michigan survey that found that one-third of high school seniors smoked, an increase of 5 percent since 1989. Most smokers develop the habit before the age of 18.

Among health components that have worsened since 1990 were an increased risk of heart disease and higher percentages of people who are obese and have sedentary lifestyles, the study said, citing statistics from the U.S. Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). More than half of Americans are overweight.

The state of Minnesota scored highest on the study's scale based on 17 health factors that include percent of high school graduates, access to prenatal care and incidence of premature death. It was followed by Utah, Hawaii, New Hampshire, Massachusetts and Wisconsin.
The states with the unhealthiest environments were Louisiana, Nevada, Mississippi, West Virginia, South Carolina and New Mexico.

Compared to a year ago, health scores in only nine states showed a positive change, while 33 states' scores declined and eight remained the same. Since 1990, however, the health score of 36 states has improved while 13 states have declined.

The positive trend was credited to the drop in the prevalence of smoking to 22.6 percent from 29.5 percent of the population, as well as decreased unemployment, improved prenatal care and reduced infant mortality rates to 8.4 deaths per 1,000 live births from 10.1 deaths.

Oregon and Alaska made the greatest strides in improving health during the period, while South Carolina, Mississippi and North Dakota residents fared the worst, hurt by reduced support for the health care system and a decline in the percentage of the population that graduated from high school.
